scenes.title: What slope makes a 90° turn?
scenes.narration: Suppose you are given y equals two x plus one, and you need a line through four comma three that is perpendicular to it. Here’s the idea: perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, so the new line must change direction in a very specific way.

scenes.title: Perpendicular means NEGATIVE RECIPROCAL
scenes.narration: For nonvertical lines, perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals. Start with two, think of it as two over one, flip it to one half, then change the sign. That gives negative one half. This is where students often mix things up: changing only the sign gives negative two, and flipping without changing the sign gives positive one half. Neither is perpendicular. The product must be negative one.

scenes.title: Use the point to place the new line
scenes.narration: Now the slope tells us the direction, but not where the line sits. The point four comma three fixes its position. Substitute x equals four and y equals three into y equals negative one half x plus b. That gives three equals negative two plus b.

scenes.title: Solve the intercept
body: Slope controls direction; b controls position
scenes.narration: Add two to both sides, so b equals five. The perpendicular line is y equals negative one half x plus five. Notice why the method works: the negative reciprocal creates the right-angle direction, and the intercept moves that line until it passes through the required point.

scenes.title: Check direction AND point
scenes.narration: Quick check: at x equals four, negative one half times four plus five equals three, so the point is on the line. And two times negative one half equals negative one, confirming the slopes are perpendicular. Recap the idea: take the negative reciprocal for the right-angle direction, then use the point to place the line. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT. Find the complete lesson below.
